issues.issue: The only oddity is the garbled date ordinal ("29\" day of December, 2006"), which does not change the identity of the parties or the date. Nothing in the naming of Prestwick KJ, LLC and Hokanson Companies, Inc. is susceptible of two readings.

The execution date of December 29, 2006 sits oddly against Paragraph 1's term "commencing on March 23, 2006", but the defect belongs to Paragraph 1 rather than to this preamble. Read against the rest of the instrument the preamble itself is consistent.

The stated duration "approximately one (1) year and eight (8) months" does not match the stated dates March 23, 2006 to December 31, 2007 (over twenty-one months), and the parenthetical defining "Buildings" is never closed. A court asked when the appointment began or ended would have to choose between the recited period and the recited dates.

The term is made to commence March 23, 2006, nine months before the Agreement's own date of December 29, 2006 in the preamble, raising a retroactivity question the instrument nowhere resolves; and the fixed December 31, 2007 expiry has no renewal or holdover provision to square with the sale-termination right in Paragraph 4(b). Whether management after 2007 was governed by this Agreement cannot be answered from the four corners.

The section contains mechanical errors that change meaning: two different subparagraphs are both lettered "(d)" (the $1,000 spending cap and the separate-account duty), so later cross-references to lettered subparagraphs are indeterminate, and the indemnity in (i) covers acts "admitted to be taken" where "omitted" is plainly meant. A court asked to apply the indemnity or a cross-reference would have to correct the text.

Subparagraph 2(i)'s indemnity of the Principal against Managing Agent negligence is hard to square with Paragraph 3(c), which obliges the Principal to carry liability insurance naming the Managing Agent as additional insured against claims arising from management and operation of the Buildings. Which party bears a negligence loss is left genuinely uncertain.

The overhead-exclusion parenthetical says overhead "shall include payroll expenses ... but shall include any premium on any insurance carried to protect any liability of another legal entity", where the second "shall include" must be "shall not include" for the sentence to make sense. As written the carve-out reverses the parties' reimbursement bargain for the employing affiliate's insurance.

The cross-references are wrong: 3(a) reimburses personnel costs "as provided in Paragraph 2(a)" when personnel is dealt with in 2(f), and refers to "the monthly accounting due ... under the terms of Paragraph 2(c)" when the monthly accounting duty is in 2(e). A court applying the reimbursement and deduction mechanics must decide which paragraphs were intended.

The amount of cover is left to "such reasonable amount as the Principal shall determine", combining a self-judging discretion with an objective reasonableness standard. If the Managing Agent were left uninsured for a claim, the adequacy of the Principal's determination is precisely what a court would construe.

The Principal's duty to insure the Managing Agent as additional insured pulls against the Managing Agent's indemnity of the Principal in Paragraph 2(i), but the two can be harmonised as covering negligence and non-negligence losses respectively. No squarely contradictory provision was found.

"Cooperate in all matters" and the Principal's right to "designate general policies" set no boundary between policy direction and day-to-day management, and the Managing Agent's "privilege and obligation of submitting recommendations" is unmeasurable. Where authority ended and breach began would turn on these words.

The Principal's policy-setting right coexists with the Managing Agent's appointment as "exclusive representative, manager and agent" in Paragraph 1 and with the binding-decision authority of the designated representative in 3(b), but these can be read together as allocating direction and execution. No irreconcilable conflict identified.

"May cancel this Agreement at the end of any calendar month after closing, upon not less than thirty (30) days' written notice" leaves the effective date ambiguous: whether cancellation takes effect at a month end at least thirty days out, or thirty days after notice. "Sold" is also undefined as to closing versus contract.

The sale-cancellation right presupposes a term still running, yet Paragraph 1 fixes expiry at December 31, 2007 with no renewal mechanism, so its operation after that date is unclear. Its relation to the Exhibit A rule excluding sale proceeds from the fee base is otherwise consistent.

The clause stacks two thirty-day periods — thirty days' prior notice of termination and a thirty-day cure period after a breach notice — without saying whether one notice can serve both, and then adds "such longer period of time as is reasonable" capped at ninety days. When termination actually becomes effective is genuinely uncertain on these words.

The "notwithstanding anything contained in this Agreement to the contrary" opener sits alongside the sale-cancellation right in 4(b) and the fixed term in Paragraph 1, but adds a right rather than contradicting them. No conflicting operative provision was found.
